en: Parivāra 20.
Sedamocanagāthā 1.
Questions on Non-Separation (Avippavāsapañhā)
There is no communal living with either monks or nuns, and in some cases,
even sharing of requisites is not permitted there; yet,
by not being separated from one's robes, there is no offense.
This question has been pondered by the wise:
it is indestructible and indivisible;
thus have five [factors] been spoken of by the Great Seer.
There is no offense for one who gives away or uses [the robe];
this question was pondered by those skilled in wisdom.
I do not speak of ten persons.
"Excluding the eleventh;
there is an offense for one who pays homage to an elder—
this question was conceived by those skilled in wisdom."
Neither one who has been suspended, nor one on probation,
neither a schismatic of the Saṅgha, nor one who has gone over to another faction;
standing on the ground of common affiliation—
How indeed might one be unique in training?
This question has been pondered by those who are skillful.
One approaches the Dhamma while inquiring about it.
Wholesome and connected with the goal,
neither living nor dead, nor extinguished—
what kind of person do the Buddhas call that?
This question was pondered by those skilled in wisdom:
"I do not speak above the collarbone,
nor below the navel."
"Under what conditions of sexual intercourse would one be defeated?
This question has been pondered by those skilled in the Dhamma."
When a bhikkhu builds a hut by means of a formal request,
if it has not been approved for its site, exceeds the proper measure,
involves destruction, or lacks sufficient space on all sides, there is no offense.
This question has been considered by those skilled in the Dhamma:
When a bhikkhu builds a hut by means of a formal request,
it must have a designated site and be of the proper measure.
It is an offense [to build] without a commencement site and without a surrounding space;
this question has been considered by those who are skilled.
One should not perform any physical exertion whatsoever.
Nor should one speak to others with words that would lead to committing a grave offense involving cutting off limbs;
this question was pondered by those skilled in wholesome states.
A virtuous person should not commit any evil by body, speech, or even by mind.
How could one who has been ruined ever truly be well-ruined?
This question was pondered by the wise:
"Without conversing with any person at all, one should not utter a word to others."
One might incur [an offense] that is verbal but not physical;
this question has been considered by those skilled in virtue.
These training rules were praised by the Best of Buddhas.
There might be four *saṅghādisesa* offenses;
one might commit them all with a single act.
This question was conceived by those skilled in wisdom.
If both [monks] have been ordained together at the same time, and one should accept a robe from the hands of both,
there may be different offenses for each.
This question was conceived by those skilled in thought:
"How might four men, acting in concert,
carry off heavy goods?"
Three are *pārājika*, one is not *pārājika*;
this question was conceived by those skilled in wisdom.
2. Questions on the *Pārājikas* and so forth.
The woman may be within,
and the monk may be outside;
there is no gap in that house.
"Due to the condition of sexual intercourse;
how could one become one who has committed a pārājika offense?
This is the question conceived by those skilled in wisdom."
If one were to take oil, honey, molasses, or even ghee by oneself and store it,
and seven days have not yet passed, [it is an offense].
For one who uses [an item] when the requisite condition exists, there is an offense.
This question has been considered by those skilled in the Dhamma.
There is an offense involving forfeiture.
If one commits [the offense] with a pure mind, it is a *pācittiya*; this question regarding those who incur [an offense] from a single [factor] has been conceived by the wise.
If twenty bhikkhus should assemble and perform an act while perceiving themselves as being in concord,
even if a bhikkhu were standing twelve yojanas away, [the act would be valid].
And that action might be subject to dispute on account of a faction;
this question has been considered by those who are wise.
Even by a mere step forward or by a word spoken, [the matter may be disturbed].
All [these] grave offenses are remediable;
one might incur sixty-four offenses at once—
this question was considered by those skilled in wisdom.
Dressed in an inner robe and wearing a double-layered outer cloak—
all of these become subject to forfeiture.
This question was conceived by those skilled in wisdom.
It is neither a formal motion (*ñatti*) nor a proclamation of the act (*kammavācā*),
nor is it "the monks," so the Victor has said.
He has no going for refuge,
yet his full ordination is unshakable;
this question was conceived by those who are skillful.
One should not kill a woman, one’s mother;
nor should one kill a man, one’s father.
A fool might kill a noble person.
And by that, one should immediately touch [the truth];
this question has been pondered by those skilled in wisdom:
"What if one were to kill his mother?"
One might slay a man who is one’s father;
having slain both mother and father,
one would not thereby incur an immediate retribution.
This question has been considered by those skilled in the Dhamma:
One should perform a formal act against someone who is not present, without having accused them and without having made them rely [on the Saṅgha].
The action may be well performed,
and yet the Saṅgha as the agent may be free from offense;
this question has been conceived by those skilled in wisdom.
Having accused and reminded him,
one should perform the formal act (kamma) in his presence;
yet the act performed would be as if unperformed.
And the Saṅgha that performs [the act] might be one that has committed an offense;
this question was conceived by those skilled in wisdom.
There is an offense for one who cuts [the robe].
There is no offense for one who cuts;
there is an offense for one who conceals;
there is no offense for one who conceals.
This question was pondered by the wise:
that one who speaks the truth incurs a heavy burden,
while one who speaks falsehood speaks lightly.
Musā speaks what is heavy,
while truth speaks what is light;
this question has been pondered by those who are skillful.
3. Questions on the Pācittiya Rules:
That which has been determined as dyed with a dye, even though it is already made allowable;
There is an offense for one who consumes it;
this question has been considered by those skilled in the Dhamma:
"When the sun has set, a monk eats meat."
He is neither insane nor deranged;
nor is he overwhelmed by pain,
and for him there is no offense.
And this Dhamma has been taught by the Sugata;
this question was conceived by me with skillful intent.
My mind is not stained by passion, nor is it possessed by a thieving thought.
Nor does he intend for another's death;
for one who gives the voting ticket there is a *chejja* offense,
and for one who receives it there is a *thullaccaya* offense.
This question has been considered by those skilled in the Dhamma:
neither is it a forest dwelling recognized as dangerous,
nor has permission been granted by the Saṅgha.
If the kaṭhina has not been spread there,
he may leave his robe and go for half a yojana;
if the dawn rises while he is still right there, there is no offense.
This question has been thought out by those skilled in the Dhamma:
all these [questions] are bodily and not vocal,
and they all have various bases.
One might commit [the offenses] simultaneously, neither before nor after;
this question has been considered by those skilled in the Dhamma.
[The offenses] are verbal, not physical.
All [offenses] have different bases;
one might commit them all together simultaneously.
This question has been considered by those who are wise.
One should not engage in sexual intercourse with three types of women,
nor with three types of men or three types of ignoble paṇḍakas;
one should not practice sexual intercourse with a man.
There might be something arising from the condition of sexual intercourse;
this is the question pondered by those skilled in wholesome states:
"Should one ask one's mother for a robe?"
And what is not dedicated to the Saṅgha;
by whom does there come to be an offense,
and when is there no offense, in the case of a relative?
This question was pondered by the wise:
How can one who is angry be successful?
How can one who is angry be censurable?
Now, what indeed is that quality by which one who is angry becomes praiseworthy?
This question has been conceived by those skilled in the Dhamma.
One who is pleased is successful;
one who is pleased is censurable.
What, then, is that Dhamma?
By whom one who is satisfied is censured—
this question was conceived by those skilled in the Dhamma.
[It concerns] the *saṅghādisesa* and the *thullaccaya*.
An offense entailing confession (pācittiya), one to be acknowledged (pāṭidesanīya),
and an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) may be incurred all at once;
this question was thought out by those who are skilled.
Both are twenty years of age;
both have one preceptor;
one teacher; one formal act (kammavācā).
One is fully ordained, one is not fully ordained;
this question was pondered by those skilled in wisdom.
It is neither made according to rule, nor dyed with a dye.
Clad in that, one may go wherever one desires; there is no offense for him,
and this is the Dhamma taught by the Sugata.
This question has been pondered by the wise:
one neither gives nor receives;
therefore, no recipient exists.
One incurs a heavy offense, not a light one,
and that is due to the cause of consumption;
this question was pondered by those skilled in wisdom.
He neither gives nor receives;
therefore, no formal acceptance exists.
He incurs a light offense, not a grave one.
And that [offense] is due to the condition of use;
this question has been considered by those skilled in the Dhamma:
"Does one incur a grave offense with remainder?"
She conceals it out of disrespect;
yet the nun would not incur an offense.
This question has been pondered by those skilled in wisdom.
The *Sedamocanagāthā* is finished. Its summary verse (*uddāna*) is:
"Non-dwelling together" and "not giving away."
Ten and the one who is not suspended;
he approaches for the Teaching with his bowl raised;
then two on account of begging.
Neither bodily weightiness, nor bodily or verbal [faults];
and training in not speaking.
Both [cases] involve four persons:
a woman, oil, and what is to be relinquished;
and a monk, and the path.
One who is clothed and has not made a formal motion shall not kill his mother or father;
whether by failing to admonish or by having admonished.
One who cuts off [defilements], possesses truth itself,
is resolute when the sun has set,
and is neither attached to robes nor to forest-dwelling.
Bodily and verbal [kamma],
the three women, and also the mother;
the angry one, the one who propitiates, and the satisfied one.
Both [types of offenses] are Saṅghādisesa.
One who does not give what has been improperly prepared incurs a heavy offense for not giving.
The verses on the drying up of the seat;
the questions analyzed by the wise.
